title: Nonverbal communication
description: Interpersonal communication through wordless (mostly visual) cues
wiki_lead:
Nonverbal communication is the transmission of messages or signals through a nonverbal platform such as eye contact (oculesics), body language (kinesics), social distance (proxemics), touch (haptics), voice (prosody and paralanguage), physical environments/appearance, and use of objects. When communicating, nonverbal channels are utilized as means to convey different messages or signals, whereas others interpret these messages. 
The study of nonverbal communication started in 1872 with the publication of The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals by Charles Darwin. Darwin began to study nonverbal communication as he noticed the interactions between animals such as lions, tigers, dogs etc. and realized they also communicated by gestures and expressions. For the first time, nonverbal communication was studied and its relevance noted. Today, scholars argue that nonverbal communication can convey more meaning than verbal communication.
In the same way that speech incorporates nonverbal components, collectively referred to as paralanguage and encompassing voice quality, rate, pitch, loudness, and speaking style, nonverbal communication also encompasses facets of one's voice. Elements such as tone, inflection, emphasis, and other vocal characteristics contribute significantly to nonverbal communication, adding layers of meaning and nuance to the conveyed message. However, much of the study of nonverbal communication has focused on interaction between individuals, where it can be classified into three principal areas: environmental conditions where communication takes place, physical characteristics of the communicators, and behaviors of communicators during interaction.
Nonverbal communication involves the conscious and unconscious processes of encoding and decoding. Encoding is defined as our ability to express emotions in a way that can be accurately interpreted by the receiver(s). Decoding is called "nonverbal sensitivity", defined as the ability to take this encoded emotion and interpret its meanings accurately to what the sender intended. Encoding is the act of generating information such as facial expressions, gestures, and postures. Encoding information utilizes signals which we may think to be universal. Decoding is the interpretation of information from received sensations given by the encoder. Culture plays an important role in nonverbal communication, and it is one aspect that helps to influence how we interact with each other.

Importance

For most communication, like giving directions, teaching math, writing books etc.. verbal information carries most of the meaning, while nonverbal communication can portray a message both vocally and with the correct body signals or gestures.  
According to some authors, nonverbal communication represents 2/3 of all communication, however this statement can be misleading due to research done by Albert Mehrabian in the 1960s, which led to the famous 7-38-55 rule: 7% words (verbal content), 38% tone of voice, & 55% facial expressions—which is close to the 2/3 claim. This rule only applies in very specific situations, such as when someone is expressing feelings or attitudes, especially when words contradict tone and facial expression. Body signals consist of physical features, conscious and unconscious gestures and signals, and the mediation of personal space. The relationship and importance of verbal and nonverbal communication changes and evolves depending on the setting and situation. When verbal communication and nonverbal gestures or cues don't make sense or work well together, the person needs to consider the history and context so that they can interpret the actual meaning of the conversation.

grok_lead: Nonverbal communication is the process by which individuals convey meaning through visual, auditory, tactile, and kinesic cues in the absence of spoken or written words, including elements such as facial expressions, gestures, posture, eye contact, touch, and vocal tone. These cues often complement, reinforce, contradict, or substitute for verbal messages, playing a pivotal role in expressing emotions, attitudes, and relational dynamics. Unlike verbal communication, nonverbal signals are frequently unintentional and operate below conscious awareness, yet they are interpreted by receivers to infer intentions and states of mind. The primary channels of nonverbal communication include the face and eyes (e.g., microexpressions and gaze direction), body movements and gestures ( kinesics), physical contact (haptics), spatial arrangement ( proxemics), and paralinguistic features like pitch, volume, and silence in voice. Additional forms encompass olfactory cues (smell) and environmental factors such as time and setting, which contribute to the overall communicative context. These channels serve multiple functions: defining the relational or situational context, accenting or commenting on verbal content, regulating conversational flow (e.g., through nods or pauses), and delivering standalone messages independent of words, such as universal emotional displays. The scientific study of nonverbal communication originated with Charles Darwin's 1872 work on emotional expressions and Sigmund Freud's insights into unconscious bodily signals, evolving into a multidisciplinary field in the mid-20th century through researchers like Edward T. Hall (proxemics), Ray Birdwhistell ( kinesics), and Paul Ekman (facial universals). It is integral to human interaction across cultures, influencing trust, dominance, and composure in relationships, as well as applications in psychology, medicine, business, and intercultural exchanges. Nonverbal cues are shaped by biological, cultural, gender, and personality factors, often conveying more nuanced relational information than words alone.
